vignette:
Kwame, at eighteen, carries a weight that belies his youthful frame. He sits, often perched on the edge of the armchair, his posture rigid, eyes darting occasionally to the door or window. Before, he was all ambition, a bright spark fresh out of secondary school, having landed a junior tax consultant position - a role he spoke of with immense pride. He loved the precision of numbers, the satisfaction of balancing ledgers, the clear-cut rules of the financial world. He was building his future, one meticulously calculated sum at a time.

The shift in his world began six months ago. He remembers the evening vividly, a Tuesday, leaving the office later than usual, the city lights blurring into streaks as he walked home. He'd taken a shortcut through a less-trafficked alley, a route he'd used countless times. The details of the attack itself are fragmented, a series of terrifying flashes: the sudden grip from behind, the rough hands, the metallic taste of fear, the overwhelming sense of powerlessness as his world dissolved into pain and humiliation. He remembers the cold concrete against his cheek, the muffled sounds, and then, the chilling silence after they left him.

In the immediate aftermath, a profound numbness settled over him. He made it home, locked the door, and for days, moved through his small apartment like a ghost. He couldn't bring himself to tell anyone, the shame a suffocating blanket. He felt dirty, broken, no longer the capable young man he knew himself to be. The thought of speaking the words aloud, of admitting what had happened, felt worse than the event itself. He started calling in sick, fabricating vague illnesses.

Now, the numbness has given way to a relentless internal storm. Sleep offers little respite; the moment his head hits the pillow, the images flood back. He sees the alley, feels the hands, hears the muffled threats. He wakes in a cold sweat, heart pounding, convinced someone is in the room. During the day, the memories ambush him without warning. A particular scent, a sudden loud noise, even the texture of certain fabrics can trigger a vivid flashback, pulling him back to that alley, his body tensing as if reliving every second. He finds himself frozen, unable to move, until the wave passes, leaving him breathless and disoriented.

His work, once a source of pride, is now a constant struggle. The meticulous detail he once loved now feels like an impossible burden. He stares at spreadsheets, the columns of numbers blurring into an incomprehensible mess. He makes errors, misses deadlines, and the structured world of tax law, which once provided a sense of control, now feels overwhelming and chaotic. He dreads client meetings, especially with older men, finding himself scrutinizing their every move, their tone of voice, a knot tightening in his stomach. He avoids eye contact, speaks in clipped sentences, and rushes through explanations, desperate to escape the interaction. His colleagues notice his withdrawal, the dark circles under his eyes, the way he flinches if someone approaches his desk unexpectedly.

He avoids the part of the city where it happened, taking long, circuitous routes home, even if it means an extra hour of travel. He no longer goes out with friends, cancelling plans at the last minute, inventing excuses. He feels perpetually on edge, hyper-alert to every sound, every shadow. The smallest unexpected noise - a car backfiring, a door slamming - sends a jolt of terror through him, his heart racing, his muscles tensing. He's become irritable, snapping at his mother when she asks about his day, then immediately regretting it, sinking deeper into a mire of guilt. He feels a constant tightness in his chest, a dull ache that never quite dissipates. He finds it impossible to feel joy, even when his younger sister achieves something wonderful. The world feels muted, colors less vibrant, laughter hollow. He just feels... empty, and very, very tired.
